Stage 5 · Grammar

Grammar

to be — am / is / are, the full picture.
1I ___ a big fan of her music.
2He ___ from South Korea.
3His teammates ___ from many countries.
4___ you Kazakh?
5She ___ American — she's Turkish.
Why

I am · he/she is · you/we/they are · negative: isn't / aren't.

1We ___ big fans of his team.
2My city ___ multicultural.
3___ they from Poland?
4I ___ from the capital city.
Why

we/they are · my city is · I am.

1We ___ big fans of his team.
2My city ___ multicultural.
3___ they from Poland?
4I ___ from the capital city.
Why

we/they are · my city is · I am.

In other words
“Shakira is a singer from Colombia.”
“Her grandparents are from Lebanon.”
“My boss isn't American, she's Turkish.”
“Are you from London?”
Notice

Notice: which words go with is, and which with are?

PersonPositiveNegativeQuestion
II am (I'm) a fan.I'm not a singer.Am I late?
he / she / itShe is Colombian.He isn't American.Is she famous?
you / we / theyThey are from Iraq.We aren't at home.Are they British?
In other words
am / is / are — for who people are, where they are from, what nationality they are.
Negative: add not — isn't, aren't, I'm not.
Question: put be first — Is she famous? Are they British?
With nationalities no “a”: She is Colombian (NOT a Colombian singer? — “a” only before a noun: a singer).
You already know the past: is → was, are → were.

most nouns+ sname → names · star → stars

Most nouns just add -s. city / country → cities / countries.
The most common irregulars: men, women, people, children — learn them as words.

Stage 8 · Listen

Listen

Track 1.2 — Godwin's multicultural lifeOriginal coursebook recording
Show transcript
Well, my name is Godwin. I'm from Nigeria originally. My wife, Sylvie, is French. Actually, she's half-French: her mother's French and her father's from Brazil. Our two children were born in England, so they're British… We speak English at home. Our home's in north London. The neighbours are a family from Iraq. Next to our house is a Polish supermarket and the restaurant across the road is Lebanese. I work for an American organization — but my boss isn't American, she's Turkish… I watch football and I play the saxophone and, oh yeah, my saxophone's Japanese.
One family, five nationalities.

Listen once. Then choose the correct answers.

1Godwin is from…
2His wife is…
3His children are…
4His boss is…
Why

Godwin — Nigeria · Sylvie — half-French · the children — British (born in England) · the boss — Turkish.

Track 1.20 — Dubai, a multicultural cityOriginal coursebook recording
Show transcript
Dubai is a very multicultural city in the United Arab Emirates. People come here to work from many different countries. Only 10% of people in Dubai are Emirati: 90% of the city's population are from other countries. Some people come from the UK and the USA, but many people are from Asia. India is home for most of Dubai's workers, but people come from Pakistan and the Philippines, too. The language of the United Arab Emirates is Arabic, but because of its international population, lots of people use English.
1How many people in Dubai are Emirati?
2The language of the UAE is…
Why

Only 10% are Emirati. The language is Arabic — but many people use English.

Stage 9 · Write

Write

Write about a famous person you like.

5–6 sentences: country, nationality, languages, why they are famous.

Useful language
  • … is a singer / footballer from…
  • He / She is… (nationality)
  • His / Her first language is…
  • He / She speaks…
  • Millions of people are fans
  • … is famous for…
Describe a famous person. Your partner guesses.

Three sentences maximum — then they guess.

Useful language
  • He / She is a…
  • He / She is from…
  • He / She is… (nationality)
  • He / She speaks…
  • His / Her fans are…
  • Is it…?
Describe a famous person. Your teacher guesses.

Three sentences maximum — then they guess.

Useful language
  • He / She is a…
  • He / She is from…
  • He / She is… (nationality)
  • He / She speaks…
  • His / Her fans are…
  • Is it…?
In other words
Step 1 — think of a famous person. Describe them: “He is a footballer. He is Portuguese. His fans are everywhere.”
Step 2 — your partner guesses. Then swap.
Step 3 — play three rounds each. Score a point for every correct guess.
